title: Profiling & diagnosis
scopeHtml: JFR, async-profiler, jcmd/jstack/jmap/jstat, GC logs, heap dumps, NMT, safepoint bias, safe production profiling, Micrometer JVM metrics, JMH, USE/RED incident method.

questions.promptHtml: What is Java Flight Recorder, and how would you run it continuously in production?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know the built-in, low-overhead production profiler rather than only "attach VisualVM".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: JFR is an event recorder built into the JVM. The JVM and JDK libraries emit typed events (GC, allocation samples, thread parks, monitor waits, I/O, CPU samples) into thread-local buffers, which are flushed to a ring of chunk files. I run it always-on with the default settings (designed for low overhead, roughly 1% by Oracle's docs, so verify on your workload) and a bounded size and age. When an incident happens I dump the last N minutes with jcmd <pid> JFR.dump and open it in JDK Mission Control or with the jfr CLI.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Open-sourced in OpenJDK 11 (JEP 328) and backported to 8u262+, so it is free on modern builds.
  • Two stock configurations in $JAVA_HOME/lib/jfr: default.jfc (continuous, low overhead) and profile.jfc (more events, lower sampling periods, higher overhead; for short windows).
  • Events are written by the emitting thread into a thread-local buffer, then promoted to global buffers and flushed to disk chunks. No stop-the-world to record. Sampling of Java stacks is periodic (about 20 ms in default, 10 ms in profile; check your jfc), and only samples threads that are in Java code or native, not at safepoint-only points, so it avoids the classic safepoint bias.
  • Continuous recording with a ring buffer: maxage and maxsize bound disk use; with disk=true the oldest chunks are deleted. You pay almost nothing until you dump.
  • JDK 14+ (JEP 349) adds event streaming so you can consume events in-process (e.g. export to metrics) without waiting for a file.
JVM threads --> thread-local buffers --> global buffers --> chunk files (ring, maxage/maxsize)
                                                         \--> JFR.dump / on-exit dump --> .jfr

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# at startup: continuous, keep 6h or 1GB, dump on exit
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=name=cont,settings=default,maxage=6h,maxsize=1g,disk=true,dumponexit=true,filename=/var/dump/app.jfr -jar app.jar

# on a live process
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=adhoc settings=profile duration=2m filename=/tmp/adhoc.jfr
jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=cont filename=/tmp/last.jfr
jfr summary /tmp/last.jfr
jfr print --events jdk.GCPhasePause,jdk.JavaMonitorEnter /tmp/last.jfr

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using profile.jfc permanently and calling it free. It is not.
  • No maxsize/maxage so the recording fills the node's ephemeral disk.
  • Starting a recording only after the incident: you lose the interesting window. Continuous is the point.
  • Treating JFR as a CPU-only tool. Its strength is correlating GC, locks, I/O and allocation on one timeline.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Default vs profile? → default is for always-on, profile has finer sampling and more events for short investigations.
  2. Can JFR show lock contention? → yes: jdk.JavaMonitorEnter and jdk.ThreadPark events with thresholds (default threshold 20 ms, so short waits are not recorded).
  3. How do you get JFR data into dashboards? → event streaming (RecordingStream, JDK 14+) or periodically dump and parse with the jfr tool.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "JFR is a profiler, start it with a flag." Senior: always-on bounded ring recording, knows thresholds hide short events, uses dumps at incident time, picks default vs profile deliberately, and knows streaming.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that had continuous JFR on every pod could dump the 10 minutes before an alert and found the culprit in minutes; a team without it had to wait for the incident to recur.

questions.promptHtml: How do you take a thread dump and what do you look for in it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Thread dumps are the first-line tool for hangs and CPU spikes; the signal is whether you can read states, not just take one.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: jcmd <pid> Thread.print (or jstack <pid>, or kill -3 which prints to stdout of the JVM). I take three dumps, 5-10 seconds apart, and compare: threads that stay in the same frame across dumps are stuck, not just passing through. I look at states (RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING), what they wait on (waiting to lock <0x...>, parking to wait for), who holds the lock, and group identical stacks to see which pool is saturated.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• A thread dump is a snapshot taken at a safepoint (so it is a stop-the-world of its own, short but not free with thousands of threads).
  • States: RUNNABLE can still mean waiting in native I/O (e.g. socketRead0) so RUNNABLE plus a socket frame is idle, not CPU. BLOCKED = waiting for a monitor. WAITING/TIMED_WAITING = Object.wait, park, sleep; parked threads in LinkedBlockingQueue.take are idle workers.
  • jstack and jcmd Thread.print report Java-level deadlocks at the bottom ("Found one Java-level deadlock"). It only covers monitors and java.util.concurrent ownable synchronizers when -l is used (jstack -l, Thread.print -l).
  • nid=0x... is the native thread id in hex; match it to top -H PIDs after converting to hex.
  • JDK 21+: jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json file includes virtual threads; the classic dump does not list them.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
for i in 1 2 3; do jcmd $PID Thread.print -l > td_$i.txt; sleep 5; done
# group by top frame
grep -A3 '"http-nio' td_1.txt | grep 'at ' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Taking one dump and concluding. A single snapshot cannot distinguish "busy" from "stuck".
  • Reading RUNNABLE as "using CPU". Socket reads show as RUNNABLE.
  • Forgetting -l, so owner of a ReentrantLock is not shown.
  • Ignoring that the dump itself pauses the JVM; do not loop it every 100 ms on a huge thread count.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Process does not respond to jstack? → attach mechanism needs a responsive JVM; try kill -3 (output goes to stdout log), or jhsdb/core dump as last resort.
  2. How do you find who holds a ReentrantLock? → -l shows "Locked ownable synchronizers"; owner thread lists it.
  3. 500 threads in the same Unsafe.park frame at pool.getTask? → idle pool workers, normal; what matters is threads in the business stack.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "run jstack, look for deadlock". Senior: multiple dumps over time, groups stacks, distinguishes native-wait RUNNABLE from CPU, correlates with top -H and with connection pools.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An outage that looked like a deadlock was 200 threads all waiting in HikariPool.getConnection; the dump pointed straight at the pool exhausted by a slow downstream.

questions.promptHtml: Which command-line JDK tools do you reach for to inspect a running JVM, and what does each answer?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks practical toolbelt breadth; seniors pick the least intrusive tool first.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: jcmd is the single entry point: Thread.print, GC.heap_dump, GC.class_histogram, VM.flags, VM.native_memory, JFR.*. jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000 gives GC occupancy and counts cheaply, with no pause. jmap -histo and -dump are the older heap tools; both can pause the JVM. I go from cheap to expensive: metrics, jstat, class histogram, JFR, then heap dump.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Tool Answers Cost
jstat -gcutil pid 1s Eden/Survivor/Old/Metaspace % and GC counts/times negligible, reads perf counters (hsperfdata)
jcmd pid GC.class_histogram which classes have most instances/bytes triggers a full GC unless -all; short pause
jcmd pid GC.heap_dump file full heap for MAT stop-the-world, size of heap on disk; dumps live objects only by default (full GC first) unless -all
jcmd pid VM.flags / VM.command_line effective flags (what ergonomics chose) negligible
jcmd pid VM.native_memory summary native memory by category (needs NMT on) small
jcmd pid Thread.print stacks short safepoint
jcmd pid JFR.* recordings low
  • jcmd replaced most uses of jstack, jmap, jinfo (these still exist). jps or jcmd with no args lists JVMs.
  • All of these use the attach API: same OS user as the target, and access to the target's temp dir (/tmp/.java_pid<pid> socket). In containers this often breaks if the user differs or /tmp is not shared.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
jstat -gcutil $PID 1000 10
jcmd $PID VM.flags
jcmd $PID GC.class_histogram | head -25
jcmd $PID GC.heap_dump -all /dump/heap.hprof   # -all: include unreachable (no full GC)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Running jmap -dump:live on a 30 GB heap under load: long pause plus a full GC; the LB then evicts the node.
  • Assuming jstat columns mean the same across collectors (ZGC/Shenandoah report differently; prefer GC logs and JFR there).
  • Dumping onto the same small disk the app writes to.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you see the flags ergonomics picked? → jcmd pid VM.flags or -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal.
  2. Why does a class histogram sometimes show fewer objects than the dump? → by default it forces a full GC first and counts live objects only.
  3. Attach fails inside the container? → run as the same UID as the JVM, shared /tmp, or use jattach; or pre-enable JFR/NMT via flags.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists the tools. Senior ranks them by intrusiveness, knows which force a GC or STW, and plans for the container attach constraints.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An on-call took a live heap dump of a 24 GB heap during peak; the node was unresponsive for ~40 s, failed health checks and was killed mid-dump, losing the evidence.

questions.promptHtml: How do you enable and read GC logs on a modern JDK, and what are the first three things you check?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: GC logs are the cheapest always-on diagnostic; reading them is a baseline senior skill.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Unified logging since JDK 9: -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m. First I check pause times against the SLO, then heap occupancy after GC (the live set trend: if "after" keeps climbing it is a leak or undersizing), then the allocation rate and the cause of each collection (Allocation Failure, G1 Humongous Allocation, Metadata GC Threshold, Evacuation Failure, full GC).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• JDK 8 used -XX:+PrintGCDetails -XX:+PrintGCDateStamps -Xloggc: (removed in 9+ in favor of -Xlog).
  • Sample G1 lines:
[2.345s][info][gc] GC(12) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 3210M->980M(8192M) 23.4ms
[9.1s][info][gc] GC(40) Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Humongous Allocation) 4100M->2900M(8192M) 31.0ms
[9.3s][info][gc] GC(41) Concurrent Mark Cycle
[41s][info][gc] GC(90) Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 8100M->7900M(8192M) 3120ms
  • Read before->after(total): after-GC value in old gen/after mixed collections is the live set. Allocation rate ~ (young_before_next - after_prev) / interval. Example: 3210M->980M at t=2.3s and next pause at 3.1s with 3190M before: (3190-980)/0.8s about 2.7 GB/s.
  • Warning signs: Full GC on G1 (should be rare), "to-space exhausted"/Evacuation Failure, back-to-back concurrent cycles (IHOP too low or live set near heap), GC time > ~5% of wall time, long Pause Remark/Cleanup with many references.
  • Tools: GCViewer, GCeasy (uploads data; check policy), or your own scripts; JFR has jdk.GarbageCollection.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: java -Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=/var/log/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m -jar app.jar

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Looking only at pause duration, not frequency or "after" occupancy.
  • Logging to stdout in a container with no rotation.
  • Mixing JDK 8 flag names into JDK 11+ (they are ignored or error).
  • Missing safepoint tag, so pauses not caused by GC are invisible.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Humongous Allocation seen? → objects >= half a G1 region; consider bigger -XX:G1HeapRegionSize or avoid huge arrays.
  2. How do you tell a leak from a big working set? → post-full-GC occupancy trend over hours.
  3. ZGC logs look different? → pauses are sub-ms; you watch allocation stalls and concurrent cycle duration instead.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "pause is 200 ms, increase heap". Senior: derives allocation rate and live set from the log, identifies the trigger cause, then decides between code change and tuning.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "GC tuning" ticket was closed after the log showed 2.7 GB/s allocation from JSON re-serialization; fixing the code beat any flag.

questions.promptHtml: What is safepoint bias in profilers, and how do JFR and async-profiler avoid it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who trust profiler output blindly from those who understand how samples are collected.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Classic profilers (e.g. Thread.getAllStackTraces-based ones, older hprof, VisualVM sampling) can only sample a thread at a safepoint, because the JVM must stop it to walk its stack consistently. Code only polls for safepoints at certain places (method returns, loop back-edges of non-counted loops), so samples cluster at those locations and hot code between polls, such as tight counted loops, looks cold. JFR and async-profiler sample using signals plus AsyncGetCallTrace-style stack walking at arbitrary points, so they are not tied to safepoints.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• A safepoint is a point where the thread state is described exactly enough for the VM to inspect or modify it (GC roots, deopt). JIT-compiled code polls a flag at specific instructions.
  • Bias consequences: time is attributed to the next poll site, not where it is spent; a long counted int loop with no poll can both skew samples and delay a stop-the-world (time-to-safepoint, TTSP).
  • Even without safepoint bias, JIT debug info only exists at certain PCs. Sampling between them is mapped to the nearest known one. -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+DebugNonSafepoints makes the JIT emit more precise debug info so JFR/async-profiler attribute to the right line/inlined frame. It has a small compile-time cost, and async-profiler recommends it for line accuracy.
  • Separate but related: TTSP stalls where one thread delays everyone. Diagnose with -Xlog:safepoint ("Safepoint ... Total: ... ms, Reaching safepoint").
  • Since JDK 10, loop strip mining reduces long counted-loop TTSP when enabled (default for G1/Parallel? verify per JDK/GC).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
java -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+DebugNonSafepoints -XX:StartFlightRecording=settings=profile -jar app.jar
java -Xlog:safepoint*:file=sp.log:uptime -jar app.jar

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing a flame graph from a safepoint-biased profiler.
  • Thinking async-profiler/JFR sample "perfectly": they have their own bias (inlining attribution, missing frames on stack overflow, skid on perf events).
  • Confusing a long GC pause with long TTSP; the safepoint log separates them.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is TTSP? → time for all threads to reach a safepoint after a request; one thread in a long loop with no poll delays everyone.
  2. Why does JFR not suffer? → it samples asynchronously and uses its own stack walker, tolerating arbitrary PCs.
  3. Does wall-clock sampling fix bias? → it fixes a different problem (off-CPU time), not attribution accuracy.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "profilers add overhead". Senior: explains polls, TTSP, DebugNonSafepoints, and cross-checks hotspots between two profilers.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: VisualVM showed HashMap.get as the top hotspot; async-profiler showed it was really a downstream JSON parse loop that never polled.

questions.contextHtml: A Spring Boot order service (8 vCPU pods, 4 GB heap, JDK 17, G1) normally runs at 35% CPU at 600 RPS. After last night's release, 3 of 12 pods sit at 95-100% CPU, p99 went from 180 ms to 2.4 s, and the other pods are fine. Errors are timeouts only; no OOM. kubectl top confirms CPU, memory flat at 2.6 GB. GC logs show Young pauses ~25 ms, one every 2 s. Release diff includes a new caching layer, a Jackson upgrade, and a changed log pattern.
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through finding what is burning the CPU.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart the pods and increase CPU limits." Or "It's GC, add heap." No evidence-driven path; hides a possible infinite loop that will recur.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it the same 3 pods since deploy or random? (points to data-dependent or per-instance state). Is it user CPU or sys/iowait? (top). Does traffic share (LB distribution) differ? Can I get a pod out of rotation without restarting? Any config difference on those pods?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Take one hot pod out of the LB (keep it alive for diagnosis), let the rest absorb the load, or roll back if the other pods are near saturation. Capture evidence first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A hot loop or catastrophic regex/parse on specific input (new cache, Jackson). (b) Cache with a bad hashCode/unbounded growth causing long linked buckets or constant eviction. (c) GC thrash (ruled out mostly: 25 ms per 2 s is ~1%). (d) Logging pattern with expensive caller-location lookup. (e) Lock spin or busy-wait.
  4. How I'd verify each: top -H -p <pid> to find the hot native thread ids, convert to hex (printf '%x\n' <tid>), then match nid=0x... in jcmd <pid> Thread.print. Three dumps 5 s apart show whether the same frames repeat. Then async-profiler asprof -d 30 -e cpu -f hot.html <pid> (or JFR with profile) for a flame graph. If the hot threads are "G1 Conc#" or "VM Thread", it is GC; otherwise application.
  5. Root cause (example outcome): Hot threads are http-nio-exec threads in java.util.regex.Pattern$... called from the new cache key normalizer; a regex with nested quantifiers backtracks exponentially on a long product code that only 3 pods' customers send (sticky routing).
  6. Fix: Short-term rollback or feature flag the normalizer. Long-term rewrite the regex (possessive/atomic groups or plain parsing), add input length limits, and a timeout wrapper where possible.
  7. Prevention: Add a perf test with adversarial input, keep continuous JFR, alert on per-pod CPU skew, lint ReDoS-prone patterns.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just add CPU (cost, hides bug); not take a heap dump (memory is flat, it is a CPU problem); not restart before capturing dumps.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Only VM Thread is hot? → Look at safepoint log; could be frequent safepoint operations (biased revoke on old JDKs, -XX:GuaranteedSafepointInterval, class redefinition).
  • top -H shows many threads each at 10%? → not a single loop; use profile, likely general hotspot like logging or serialization.
  • Cannot attach in the container? → kubectl debug with a shared process namespace, or use the pre-enabled JFR flag.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a "harmless" validation regex ran fine on test data for months, then one tenant uploaded 10 KB strings and three pods pinned at 100% for an hour. The thread dump was the giveaway: identical Pattern$Loop.match frames on all hot threads in three dumps.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts or scales without evidence; proposes heap changes.
  • Hire: uses top -H + hex nid + jstack, then a flame graph; identifies the hot code.
  • Strong hire: also isolates the pod first, rules out GC with numbers, explains why only some pods, and designs prevention (adversarial tests, per-pod skew alerts).

questions.promptHtml: Explain async-profiler's cpu, wall, alloc and lock modes. When do you use each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Picking the wrong mode is the most common reason a profile "shows nothing" while the service is slow.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CPU mode samples threads that are actually running on a CPU, so it answers "where is CPU going". Wall-clock mode samples all threads at a fixed interval regardless of state (running, sleeping, blocked), so it answers "where does a request spend its time", which is what I need for latency with I/O or lock waits. Alloc mode samples allocations (via TLAB events) to find who creates garbage. Lock mode samples contended monitor and ReentrantLock waits, to find who blocks whom.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• CPU sampling: default 10 ms of CPU time (100 Hz) using perf_events where available, falling back to itimer. Idle threads never show up, so a service that waits on a database shows a nearly empty profile.
  • Wall mode (-e wall, usually with -t per-thread): every thread is sampled every interval. Flame graph width is time, including blocked time. Filter by a request thread name to see the full latency anatomy.
  • Alloc mode (-e alloc or --alloc 512k): samples roughly one allocation per interval of allocated bytes, not per object, so it is proportional to bytes. Intervals smaller than the TLAB size do not take effect as the sampling hooks TLAB refills and outside-TLAB allocations. Output shows allocation sites, not live retention.
  • Lock mode (--lock 10ms): reports contended monitor enters and park waits; width is wait time.
  • Multiple modes can be combined only in JFR output.
Symptom                         Mode
CPU 90%, hot code?              cpu
p99 high, CPU low               wall (-t)
GC churn, high alloc rate       alloc
threads BLOCKED / waiting       lock

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
asprof -d 30 -e cpu   -f cpu.html  <pid>
asprof -d 30 -e wall -t -f wall.html <pid>
asprof -d 30 -e alloc --alloc 512k -f alloc.html <pid>
asprof -d 30 --lock 10ms -f lock.html <pid>
asprof -d 60 -e cpu --alloc 2m --lock 10ms -o jfr -f all.jfr <pid>

(Older releases use profiler.sh instead of asprof; options may vary by version, so check asprof --help.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• CPU profile on an I/O-bound service: blames the 3% that runs.
  • Wall mode without -t/thread filter: idle pool threads dominate the graph.
  • Reading alloc graph as memory leak; it shows allocation rate, not retention. Use a heap dump for leaks.
  • Profiling for 5 seconds on a spiky workload.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can't I get CPU samples in a locked-down container? → perf_events may be blocked (perf_event_paranoid, seccomp); async-profiler falls back to itimer or you use wall mode; verify on your platform.
  2. Difference between JFR's execution sampler and async-profiler? → JFR's samples are limited per interval and Java frames only; async-profiler shows native/kernel frames too.
  3. How do you profile only startup? → -agentpath / asprof start at launch with wall mode.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "I take a CPU flame graph". Senior: picks mode from the symptom, uses wall + per-thread for latency, combines alloc with GC logs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service at 20% CPU had p99 of 1.5 s; the CPU profile was empty, the wall profile showed 70% of time in a synchronized logging appender.

questions.promptHtml: How do you read a flame graph, and what are the common misreadings?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Reading profiles correctly is the core profiling skill.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The x-axis is not time order; it is sample count, so frame width is the share of samples (time or bytes, depending on mode) that included that frame in the stack. The y-axis is stack depth: callers below, callees above. I look for wide plateaus at the top (self time) and wide towers in the middle (cumulative cost). I never judge by height. I compare before/after with a differential graph.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Sibling frames are sorted alphabetically, so left-to-right carries no meaning.
  • Self time = width of a frame minus the widths of its children. Wide top edge = function where time is spent; wide frame with many narrow children = cost spread across callees (fix the caller).
  • Inlining: JIT inlines callees, so frames may be missing or attributed to the caller unless -XX:+DebugNonSafepoints and inlined-frame reconstruction are used (async-profiler does reconstruct inlined frames from debug info).
  • Native and JVM frames: [unknown], libjvm.so frames like G1ParScanThread show GC; Interpreter and compiler threads (C2Compiler) show warm-up cost.
  • Wall vs CPU graphs differ: in wall graphs Unsafe.park, epoll_wait plateaus are waits, not work.
  • Use collapsed stacks and diff (e.g. jfrconv, FlameGraph's difffolded.pl) to compare builds.
 [ HashMap.get  ][ parse ]            <- top = self time
 [   handle()     ][  send()  ]
 [        doFilter()          ]
 [            run()           ]       <- bottom = root

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking the left side happened earlier.
  • Optimizing the tallest tower instead of the widest function.
  • Comparing two graphs of different durations without normalizing.
  • Ignoring GC and compiler frames that eat share during warmup.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A frame is 40% wide but self time ~0? → it is a coordinator; look at its children.
  2. What is an icicle graph? → the same data inverted (root on top).
  3. How do you prove a fix helped? → differential flame graph or compare same-load profiles plus latency metrics.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "red means hot". Senior: knows color is meaningless, differentiates self vs cumulative, mode-specific interpretation, and uses diffs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After "optimizing" the tallest stack, a team saw no change because that stack was narrow; the wide plateau was an innocuous-looking String.format in a logger.

questions.contextHtml: A pricing API (JDK 21, G1, 6 GB heap, 4 vCPU pods, 40 pods at 1,200 RPS each) costs too much. Finance wants 30% fewer pods. CPU averages 70%, p99 is 140 ms and spikes to 400 ms every few seconds. GC log excerpt: Pause Young (Normal) 2800M->310M(6144M) 18ms every ~1.1 s. Live set after mixed GC is stable at ~900 MB. Old gen is healthy. Someone proposes switching to ZGC and adding more heap.
questions.promptHtml: How do you decide what to do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch to ZGC, it is lower latency." That ignores that the real issue is a high allocation rate; ZGC trades CPU for pauses and may increase pod count.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the SLO and which spike is it (the 400 ms)? Is p99 spike aligned with GC pauses? CPU split user vs GC threads? Is CPU or p99 the binding constraint for pod count? Any recent change in payload size?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; this is optimization. Freeze flag changes until I have data.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) High allocation rate from per-request objects (JSON trees, string concatenation, boxed collections). Math: 2800 MB - 310 MB = ~2.5 GB per 1.1 s = about 2.3 GB/s, i.e. ~1.9 MB per request at 1,200 RPS, which is huge for a pricing call. (b) GC CPU share: 18 ms per 1.1 s is only ~1.6% of wall, so pauses do not explain 70% CPU. (c) The 400 ms spikes are from something else: retry storms, a lock, a downstream. (d) JIT deopt or huge payload outliers.
  4. How I'd verify each: async-profiler alloc mode (-e alloc --alloc 256k -d 60) and a JFR recording (jdk.ObjectAllocationSample, jdk.GarbageCollection) on one canary; CPU flame graph; correlate p99 spikes with GC log timestamps and jdk.ThreadPark.
  5. Root cause (example): 55% of allocated bytes come from deserializing a 400 KB catalog response into a JsonNode tree and then mapping to POJOs per request; 15% from String.format in logging at INFO. The 400 ms spikes correlate with a 3 s catalog refresh that holds a lock, not with GC.
  6. Fix: Short-term: cache the parsed catalog snapshot (immutable, swapped atomically), disable the INFO log format. Long-term: stream parsing or a binary protocol, reuse buffers. Then re-measure: if allocation drops 70%, CPU drops and I can cut pods. Reconsider the collector only after.
  7. Prevention: Allocation rate and GC overhead dashboards (jvm.gc.memory.allocated), perf test budget in bytes per request, JMH checks on hot mappers.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not switching to ZGC first (generational ZGC in 21 is good but costs CPU/barrier overhead; also would not cut allocation); not enlarging young gen blindly (less frequent but not cheaper pauses, and larger cache misses). Not trusting a 60 s profile from a single pod without checking representativeness.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would larger young gen reduce CPU? → Marginally: fewer GCs, same allocation work; zeroing and cache effects remain.
  • What if alloc profile points into a library? → Check config (e.g., reuse mappers/ObjectReader), or swap; measure with JMH.
  • How do you prove cost savings? → Load test with a fixed RPS per pod comparing CPU%, p99, and GC overhead before/after.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite case: a team spent two sprints on GC flags with no gain. A one-hour alloc profile showed a per-request ObjectMapper constructed in a helper. Fixing one line cut allocation 40% and saved 8 pods.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: changes collector/heap without measuring.
  • Hire: computes allocation rate, uses alloc profiling, distinguishes GC cost from CPU cost.
  • Strong hire: also separates the p99 spikes as an independent cause, ties the fix to pod count and cost, and sets a regression guard.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the heap dump workflow for an OutOfMemoryError: capture, analysis in MAT, and what to look at.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Leak diagnosis is a core senior skill; interviewers want the vocabulary (shallow vs retained, dominator tree, GC roots) and operational safety.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Prefer -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=... so you get the dump at the failure point; otherwise jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump. Open it in Eclipse MAT, run the Leak Suspects report, then use the dominator tree sorted by retained heap, and "path to GC roots excluding weak/soft references" for the suspect. I compare two dumps taken hours apart to separate leak from large working set.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Shallow size = memory of the object itself. Retained size = memory freed if the object were collected (everything only reachable through it). Dominator tree orders objects by retained size, so one ConcurrentHashMap dominating 70% is the lead.
  • GC roots: thread stacks, static fields, JNI refs, class loaders. A leak is an unwanted path from a root. "Path to GC roots" shows it.
  • MAT needs memory about the dump size: parse a 20 GB dump with the headless ParseHeapDump.sh on a big machine, then open the generated indexes.
  • Dump size roughly equals used heap; a full dump is stop-the-world and can take tens of seconds per 10 GB (depends on disk).
  • Histogram diff between two dumps: look for classes whose counts grow monotonically (byte[], HashMap$Node, your domain class).
  • Sensitive data: dumps contain secrets and PII; handle as sensitive.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
java -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError -jar app.jar
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /dumps/h1.hprof
./ParseHeapDump.sh h1.hprof org.eclipse.mat.api:suspects org.eclipse.mat.api:overview

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Dumping on the same volume as the logs/data and filling the disk; in Kubernetes the pod's ephemeral storage limit evicts the pod during the dump.
  • ExitOnOutOfMemoryError without a dump path on a persistent volume: dump is lost with the pod.
  • Blaming byte[]/String at the top; they are leaves. Find the owner via dominator tree.
  • Not distinguishing weak/soft refs when computing roots.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Dump too big for a laptop? → headless parsing on a server, or analyze histograms with jcmd GC.class_histogram.
  2. How would you detect a ThreadLocal leak in MAT? → look at Thread.threadLocals (ThreadLocalMap$Entry) with large values, in pool threads.
  3. Can you find a leak without a heap dump? → JFR jdk.OldObjectSample with path-to-gc-roots (path-to-gc-roots=true on JFR.start/dump) gives low-overhead leak candidates.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "open it in MAT, find the biggest object". Senior: dominator + retained size, two-dump diff, safe capture in Kubernetes, security of dumps, and OldObjectSample as a lighter alternative.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A listener list registered per request and never removed retained 300 MB of request contexts; the dominator tree showed an ArrayList in a singleton, named in a single click.

questions.promptHtml: The container RSS is far above the Java heap size. How does Native Memory Tracking help, and what does it not cover?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Container OOM-kills with a healthy heap are a classic senior-level problem; the signal is knowing the JVM's non-heap consumers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The process uses heap plus metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, GC data structures, symbol tables, direct buffers, and malloc arenas. NMT (-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary) tracks what the JVM itself allocates, by category. I take a baseline, wait, then run summary.diff to see which category grows. It does not see native allocations from JNI libraries, glibc fragmentation, or mmap-ed files outside the JVM's accounting, which I check with pmap, /proc/<pid>/smaps, and malloc tuning.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• NMT is off by default. It has some overhead (Oracle documents about 5-10% for summary and detail modes in recent docs, verify for your JDK). It can't be turned on later without a restart; shutdown stops tracking.
  • Categories: Java Heap, Class (metadata), Thread (stacks), Code, GC, Compiler, Internal, Symbol, Native Memory Tracking itself, Arena Chunk, etc. Direct ByteBuffers show under "Other" (JDK 17+) or "Internal" (older).
  • Reconcile: RSS ≈ NMT committed + non-JVM native + page cache differences. NMT shows committed, not RSS, so also read jcmd pid VM.native_memory summary alongside container metrics.
Source Visible to NMT?
Heap, metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, GC structures yes
Unsafe.allocateMemory, direct ByteBuffer yes (Other/Internal)
JNI malloc in third-party libs (Netty native, RocksDB, zstd) no
glibc malloc arena fragmentation no (appears as RSS higher than committed)
  • Mitigations for glibc: MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 (or 4) env var; consider jemalloc. Mention as a common pattern, measure before/after.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary -jar app.jar
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline
# later
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Enabling NMT only after the OOM-kill, with nothing to diff.
  • Assuming NMT sum equals RSS.
  • Setting -Xmx equal to the container limit; leave room (e.g. heap 50-70% of limit via -XX:MaxRAMPercentage, adjust to workload).
  • Forgetting thread count: 500 threads x 1 MB default stack is 500 MB of reserved (committed gradually).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize interact? → caps direct ByteBuffers; default equals max heap size, so total can exceed what you budgeted.
  2. How do you find a JNI leak? → NMT stays flat while RSS grows; use pmap, jemalloc profiling, or LD_PRELOAD tools.
  3. Overhead concerns for prod? → use summary rather than detail; test the cost.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "increase memory limit". Senior: breaks RSS into categories, uses NMT diff, knows its blind spots, and budgets non-heap memory up front.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Pods were OOMKilled every 3 days with 55% heap used; NMT diff showed thread arena growth plus glibc fragmentation in a Netty-heavy service. MALLOC_ARENA_MAX stabilized RSS.

questions.contextHtml: A Kotlin/Spring service (JDK 17, 3 GB container limit, -Xmx2g, G1) restarts every ~18 hours with OOMKilled (exit 137). Grafana: heap used oscillates 0.9-1.7 GB with healthy GC; no OutOfMemoryError in logs; no heap dump exists. Container working set climbs ~35 MB/hour from 1.9 GB to 3.0 GB. The service uses Netty-based HTTP clients, Kafka client, and Jackson. Someone says "heap must be leaking, bump -Xmx to 2.5g".
questions.promptHtml: How do you find the cause and fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Raises -Xmx (which worsens it: the non-heap budget shrinks). Or demands a heap dump even though the heap is not the problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does MaxDirectMemorySize get set? How many threads (jvm.threads.live) and does it grow? Does metaspace or code cache grow? Has traffic mix changed? Which JDK build and base image (glibc vs musl)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Lower -Xmx to leave headroom (e.g. 1.5g with the live set ~0.9g after GC; verify), or raise the container limit temporarily; add -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError and a restart schedule if needed. Do not raise Xmx.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Direct buffer growth from Netty/NIO (pooled arenas, unreleased ByteBuf). (b) Native allocator fragmentation (glibc arenas) from many threads. (c) Thread count growth (unbounded executor), each with stack plus TLAB. (d) Metaspace/classloader leak (dynamic proxies). (e) Code cache fill or GC native structures.
  4. How I'd verify each: Restart one canary with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary; jcmd VM.native_memory baseline, then summary.diff after a few hours. Compare with Micrometer jvm.buffer.memory.used{id=direct}, jvm.threads.live, jvm.memory.used{area=nonheap}. pmap -x / /proc/pid/smaps_rollup for RSS. Enable Netty leak detector (-Dio.netty.leakDetection.level=advanced) in staging.
  5. Root cause (example): NMT shows committed memory flat except Other (direct) growing; Netty pooled arena retains buffers because one client path doesn't release response ByteBufs on error. RSS grows 35 MB/hour; once heap + non-heap hits 3 GB, the kernel OOM-kills.
  6. Fix: Short-term: cap -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize and reduce Xmx so a budget exists (2 GB heap + ~600 MB non-heap + direct cap would not fit in 3 GB; recompute: e.g. Xmx 1.5g, direct cap 256m, metaspace/code/threads ~400m). Long-term: fix the release path (ReferenceCountUtil.release in finally) and add the leak detector test.
  7. Prevention: Alert on container_memory_working_set_bytes / limit > 85%, a memory budget table per service, canary soak test of 24 hours, MaxRAMPercentage instead of absolute Xmx where sizing varies.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not increasing Xmx; not enabling NMT detail in prod without testing overhead; not assuming musl vs glibc without checking; not dropping -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch casually (affects RSS accounting at startup).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• NMT is flat but RSS grows? → native library or allocator fragmentation: try MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2, jemalloc, and pmap deltas.
  • Do we need a heap dump? → Not for this; heap is healthy and the dump shows direct buffer wrappers at most.
  • Why doesn't the JVM throw OOM before the kernel kills? → The JVM only knows its own limits (Xmx, direct cap); the cgroup limit is enforced by the kernel, so the process can be killed without a JVM error.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: an image resizing sidecar JNI library leaked 40 KB per request. Heap graphs were perfect, NMT flat, and RSS rose linearly. The giveaway was correlation with request count and the fact that pods with lower traffic lasted longer.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases heap or asks for a heap dump.
  • Hire: identifies non-heap memory, uses NMT diff and metrics.
  • Strong hire: separates NMT-visible vs invisible, budgets the container, explains why no JVM OOM occurs, and sets alerting and soak tests.

questions.promptHtml: How do you profile a production JVM safely, especially inside a container?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors must diagnose live systems without causing a second incident.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I use low-overhead, sampling tools and time-box them: JFR (default settings continuous, profile for a bounded window) or async-profiler for 30-60 s on one canary pod, not the whole fleet. I take the pod out of the LB if the tool pauses (heap dump, class histogram). In containers I verify the attach path works (same UID, /tmp), that the profiler has needed permissions (perf_events may be blocked, so I use itimer/wall), and that output goes to a volume with space. I pre-enable what cannot be turned on later (NMT, JFR flags, GC logs).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Cost ladder: metrics (free) < GC logs (near free) < JFR default (low) < async-profiler sampling (low, but wall mode with many threads costs more) < thread dumps (short safepoint) < class histogram (forces GC) < heap dump (STW, proportional to heap) < debugger/instrumenting agents (high).
  • Containers: the attach API uses a UNIX socket in /tmp of the target's mount namespace; running a debug container requires shareProcessNamespace and matching UID, or kubectl exec into the app container if the image has JDK tools (a JRE-only image has no jcmd; consider JDK image or jattach).
  • Kernel permissions: perf_events needs kernel.perf_event_paranoid and capabilities (often SYS_ADMIN/PERFMON), which hardened clusters block. async-profiler then falls back to itimer-based sampling. Verify behavior for your version.
  • Always have a rollback: stop profiler (asprof stop, JFR.stop) and a time limit (-d, duration=).
  • Data hygiene: JFR and heap dumps contain secrets (request payloads, tokens); restrict access.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
kubectl debug -it pod/app-7 --image=eclipse-temurin:21-jdk --target=app --share-processes -- bash
asprof -d 30 -e cpu -f /tmp/cpu.html $(pgrep -f app.jar)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Running profile.jfc plus allocation profiling on every pod.
  • Dumping the heap on a pod already near its memory limit (dump process buffers can push ephemeral storage or memory).
  • Profiling a pod that is not the bad one.
  • Leaving a recording unbounded.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can async-profiler be attached at startup? → yes via -agentpath: with start,event=cpu,file=....
  2. How to profile without shell access? → bake JFR flags in, expose a protected actuator/JMX endpoint to dump, or a sidecar.
  3. How do you limit blast radius? → canary one pod, time-box, alert if latency worsens, auto-stop.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "attach VisualVM remotely". Senior: ranks tools by overhead, plans for container constraints, pre-enables what cannot be added later, and secures artifacts.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A remote JMX + sampling profiler session on a hot pod added 30% CPU and tipped the node over; JFR dump from a continuous recording would have been free.

questions.promptHtml: Which JVM metrics do you put on a dashboard and alert on for a Java service, and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can see trouble coming before an incident, using actual Micrometer meter names.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Memory: jvm.memory.used/max by pool and jvm.gc.live.data.size (live set after GC) trend; GC: jvm.gc.pause rate and max, jvm.gc.memory.allocated (allocation rate) and jvm.gc.memory.promoted; threads: jvm.threads.live, jvm.threads.states (blocked/waiting); buffers: jvm.buffer.memory.used (direct); classes: jvm.classes.loaded; CPU: process.cpu.usage, system.cpu.usage; plus pool-level metrics: executor.queued, executor.active, hikaricp.connections.pending, and request latency percentiles. I alert on symptoms (latency, errors, saturation) and keep the JVM metrics as diagnosis panels, with a few leading indicators.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Leading indicators: live set after GC trending up (leak), GC time ratio over ~5-10% (rate(jvm_gc_pause_seconds_sum[1m])), allocation rate spikes, old gen > 80% after mixed GC, thread count rising monotonically, direct buffers rising, metaspace rising.
  • jvm.memory.used includes non-heap areas (area=nonheap, id Metaspace, CodeCache), which matter for container memory.
  • jvm.gc.live.data.size and jvm.gc.max.data.size are meaningful for generational collectors (old gen after collection).
  • Saturation: jvm.threads.states{state="blocked"}, executor.queued (queue depth), Hikari pending, Tomcat tomcat.threads.busy vs tomcat.threads.config.max.
  • Container: compare container_memory_working_set_bytes against limits, not only JVM memory.
  • Cardinality: keep tags few; don't tag by user id.
Question Metric
Leak? jvm.gc.live.data.size trend
GC overhead? jvm.gc.pause sum rate
Allocation pressure? jvm.gc.memory.allocated rate
Thread leak / contention? jvm.threads.live, states
Native/direct? jvm.buffer.memory.used, working set
Pool saturation? executor.queued, hikaricp.connections.pending

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Alerting on "heap used > 80%": heap use with a lazy collector is naturally high before GC. Alert on post-GC live set.
  • Averaging pause times; watch max and p99.
  • No per-pod view; one bad pod hides in a fleet average.
  • Metric names and existence differ with collector (e.g. ZGC and Shenandoah); verify per setup.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you compute GC overhead? → rate(jvm_gc_pause_seconds_sum[5m]) as a fraction of wall time (and concurrent GC CPU separately).
  2. How to detect thread leaks early? → alert on jvm.threads.live slope/absolute vs expected.
  3. Why is the metrics scrape not enough in an incident? → low resolution; need GC logs/JFR for the ms-level story.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists heap and CPU. Senior alerts on post-GC live set, allocation rate, saturation of pools, and links JVM metrics with container limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A slowly rising jvm.gc.live.data.size flagged a leak 9 days before it would have OOMed, caught by a slope alert.

questions.promptHtml: What are the USE and RED methods, and how do you apply them to a Java service incident?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you have a structured method, not tool-hopping.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) describes request-facing symptoms of a service; USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) examines every resource: CPU, memory, disk, network, plus software resources like thread pools and connection pools. I start with RED to confirm user impact and which endpoint, then walk USE across resources to find the saturated one, then drill into the JVM with the right tool.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• RED (Tom Wilkie) suits request-driven services; USE (Brendan Gregg) suits resources.
  • For a JVM service the resources are: CPU (utilization %, run queue = saturation), heap (live set % of max, GC time = saturation), threads (busy/max, queue), connection pools (active/max, pending waiters), file descriptors, network, downstream calls.
  • Procedure: (1) define impact (RED, from the user's perspective); (2) find where it started (deploy, traffic, dependency); (3) USE sweep to find the saturated resource; (4) form a hypothesis; (5) confirm with a profiler/dump; (6) mitigate; (7) fix.
  • Saturation is the key that Utilization hides: a pool at 100% active with 200 waiters is the problem even though "CPU is only 20%".
RED: rate down? errors up? duration up?  -> which endpoint, since when
USE: CPU / heap+GC / threads / DB pool / downstream  -> which is saturated
Then: dump / flame graph / JFR to explain WHY

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Jumping into a heap dump when the symptom is pool starvation.
  • Checking only utilization.
  • Skipping "what changed".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does Little's law fit? → concurrency = arrival rate x latency; explains pool saturation.
  2. What is the "four golden signals"? → latency, traffic, errors, saturation (Google SRE).
  3. How do you apply USE to a thread pool? → utilization = active/max, saturation = queue length or rejections, errors = rejected/failed tasks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: checks logs randomly. Senior: user impact first, then structured resource sweep including software resources, then a targeted tool.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "slow DB" incident was really hikaricp.connections.pending > 0 from a leaked connection in one code path; USE sweep found it in minutes.

questions.contextHtml: Black Friday, 15:02. A checkout service (JDK 17, 16 pods x 4 vCPU, G1 4 GB heap, Tomcat max 200 threads, Hikari 30 connections) sees p99 jump from 220 ms to 6 s; error rate 4% (timeouts, 503s from the gateway). RPS is 2.5x normal. CPU per pod is 45%. GC: pauses < 40 ms. No deploys in 24 hours. Alerts channel is noisy. The on-call has already restarted two pods and it didn't help. The CTO is on the call.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the diagnosis. What's your sequence and what do you say to the room?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Starts guessing (GC, DB, network) and runs random commands; or restarts everything; or scales pods without understanding a saturated dependency.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed (traffic mix, feature flags, dependency health, config)? Which endpoints are slow vs fine? Is it uniform across pods? Downstream latency (DB, payment provider) dashboards? Time of first symptom vs traffic ramp?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Protect the system: shed load (rate limit non-critical endpoints), enable circuit breakers/fallbacks, disable expensive features via flags, scale only if a resource (not a dependency) is saturated. Stop restarting pods (it drops warm JIT/caches and worsens it).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Connection pool saturation due to a slow dependency (Little's law: 30 connections at 100 ms per query can serve 300 qps per pod; if latency goes to 1 s, only 30 qps/pod). (b) Tomcat thread exhaustion (200 threads waiting on pool or downstream). (c) GC (ruled out by 40 ms pauses). (d) Lock contention in the app. (e) CPU throttling (cgroup quota) invisible in usage graphs.
  4. How I'd verify each: RED per endpoint, then USE: hikaricp.connections.pending/active, tomcat.threads.busy, jvm.threads.states, downstream timers. One thread dump on a bad pod: count threads in HikariPool.getConnection vs socketRead in the payment client. container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods for throttling. A 30 s wall-clock async-profiler run on one pod for where request threads wait.
  5. Root cause (example): Payment provider's p99 rose to 4 s; 190 of 200 Tomcat threads sit in the payment HTTP client with a 30 s timeout; Hikari connections held while waiting on the payment call inside a transaction, so pending hit 120. CPU is only 45% because threads are blocked, not working.
  6. Fix: Short-term: reduce payment client timeout to ~2 s with a circuit breaker and fail fast/degrade (queue the payment), release DB connection before the external call. Long-term: bulkhead per dependency (separate pool), async/virtual threads for the call, backpressure and load shedding, timeouts budget per request.
  7. Prevention: Saturation alerts on pools, timeout budgets in design review, game-day with slow dependency injection, a runbook following RED/USE.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not scaling pods (more pods = more pressure on the DB/payment provider); not raising Hikari max (moves the problem to the database); not restarting; not a heap dump or tuning GC.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Provider owns the problem and cannot fix it? → degrade gracefully: async confirmation, queue and retry with idempotency keys.
  • How do you decide the timeout value? → from the dependency's p99 under normal load plus a budget derived from the request's overall deadline; never above the caller's timeout.
  • Gateway retries make it worse? → retry storms amplify; limit retries, use jitter and budgets.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite event: restart waves during a dependency brownout made everything worse because cold JVMs took 90 s to warm up. The calm approach, shedding load and cutting timeouts, restored service in 4 minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: guesses and restarts; blames GC.
  • Hire: RED then USE, finds pool/thread saturation, uses Little's law, mitigates with timeouts.
  • Strong hire: communicates clearly, avoids amplifying actions, covers bulkheads, load shedding, retry amplification and prevention.

questions.promptHtml: Why can't you benchmark Java code with a main and System.nanoTime() loop, and what does JMH do about it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Microbenchmark literacy shows you understand the JIT.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The JIT changes the code as it runs: interpreter first, then C1, then C2 after profiling, with inlining and deoptimization. A naive loop measures warm-up, may get the whole computation eliminated if the result is unused (dead-code elimination), or have inputs constant-folded. JMH forks fresh JVMs, runs warmup iterations before measured ones, provides Blackhole to consume results, @State for non-constant inputs, and reports score with error.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Defaults: JMH runs warmup and measurement iterations with defined time per iteration; defaults have been reported as 5 warmup and 5 measurement iterations of 10 s each (verify for your JMH version), with forks configurable via @Fork.
  • Fork: new JVM per fork avoids profile pollution from earlier benchmarks (where a shared call site becomes megamorphic).
  • Modes: Throughput, AverageTime, SampleTime (percentiles), SingleShotTime (cold start).
  • Pitfalls: dead code elimination, constant folding (use @State fields, non-final), loop optimizations (don't loop inside the benchmark manually; use @OperationsPerInvocation when you must), false sharing between threads in multi-threaded benchmarks, unrealistic data (sorted input, tiny working set fits L1 cache), and measuring GC-allocated garbage without the -prof gc profiler.
  • Profilers: -prof gc (allocation rate bytes/op), -prof perfasm, -prof async for flame graphs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@State(Scope.Thread)
@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
@Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 2)
@Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 2)
@Fork(2)
public class ParseBench {
    String input = "2024-05-01T10:15:30Z"; // non-final: not folded
    @Benchmark
    public Instant parse() { return Instant.parse(input); } // return value = consumed
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Benchmarks that return void and discard results.
  • Comparing results from different machines or noisy laptops with turbo/thermal throttling.
  • Trusting a 3% difference within error bars.
  • Concluding from a microbenchmark that the service gets faster; real code has cache misses, contention and GC.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does Blackhole.consume do? → prevents the JIT from proving a value unused without adding meaningful cost.
  2. When is JMH the wrong tool? → end-to-end latency, I/O-bound paths; use load tests (k6, wrk2) and profiling.
  3. How to see allocation? → -prof gc.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "JMH warms up". Senior: lists specific pitfalls (DCE, folding, profile pollution, data shape), uses -prof gc/async, and restricts conclusions to the micro level.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "faster" custom parser benchmarked 4x quicker but showed no gain in the service: the benchmark used one tiny constant input, hiding branch mispredictions and allocation of real payloads.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate benchmarks two ways to join IDs and reports "approach B is 40x faster, merge it". The code:

public class JoinBench {
    static final List<String> IDS = List.of("a1", "b2", "c3", "d4");

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) joinA(); // warm-up
        long t = System.nanoTime();
        for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; i++) joinA();
        long a = System.nanoTime() - t;
        t = System.nanoTime();
        for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; i++) joinB();
        long b = System.nanoTime() - t;
        System.out.println("A=" + a / 1e6 + "ms B=" + b / 1e6 + "ms");
    }
    static String joinA() { String s = ""; for (String id : IDS) s += id + ","; return s; }
    static String joinB() { return String.join(",", IDS); } // result discarded by callers
}

Machine: a laptop on battery, JDK 17. The JVM was started once and both loops ran in the same process.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with this benchmark and how would you redo it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks fine, B uses a library so it's faster", or only says "add warm-up". Misses dead-code elimination and shared-JVM profile effects.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What decision depends on this (hot path or not)? Real input sizes (4 IDs or 400)? Is allocation/GC a concern? What are the target latencies?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident: block the merge justification until there is valid data; don't claim 40x.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Dead-code elimination: results are discarded and joinB has no side effects, so C2 may remove it; joinA has a different shape, so the difference measures elimination. (b) Constant input (static final List.of) allows folding/escape analysis; not representative. (c) Single run in one JVM: no forks, OSR compilation of main's loops, order effects (A runs first, B inherits warmed JIT). (d) Insufficient warm-up for C2 plus GC differences unmeasured. (e) Laptop on battery: CPU frequency scaling.
  4. How I'd verify each: Rewrite as JMH with @Benchmark returning the string, @State data, -prof gc, 2+ forks; also run B first and A second to see order effects; compare on a plugged-in, quiet machine. Check generated code with -XX:+PrintCompilation if needed, or -prof perfasm.
  5. Root cause: The harness measures JIT behavior and removed code rather than the join operations; the 40x is an artifact. In reality String.join vs += in a loop differ modestly for 4 short items (javac compiles += to StringConcatFactory on 9+ or StringBuilder on 8), and the larger difference is allocation per iteration, which only shows in -prof gc.
  6. Fix:
@State(Scope.Benchmark)
public class JoinBench {
    @Param({"4", "64"}) int n;
    List<String> ids;
    @Setup public void setup() { ids = IntStream.range(0, n).mapToObj(i -> "id" + i).toList(); }
    @Benchmark public String join() { return String.join(",", ids); }
    @Benchmark public String concat() { String s = ""; for (String id : ids) s += id + ","; return s; }
}
  1. Prevention: Team template for JMH, checklist (returns/Blackhole, no constants, forks, params, gc profiler), require service-level evidence for performance PRs.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't micro-optimize a path that profiling doesn't show hot; I'd not run JMH on shared CI runners with noisy neighbours and treat it as precise.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Both benchmarks within 2% under JMH? → difference within error; don't claim; look at allocation or choose readability.
  • Where does Blackhole matter vs return? → return handles one value; Blackhole for several values.
  • Real services are slower than the micro predicted? → cache misses, GC, contention, real input sizes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite case: a "5x faster" serializer turned out to be benchmarking the same cached object each time; with real payload variance it was 8% faster and used 3x more memory.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: trusts the numbers.
  • Hire: names DCE, warm-up/forks, constants; proposes JMH.
  • Strong hire: also notes order effects, OSR, hardware noise, -prof gc, parameterization, and ties results back to a profile of the actual service.

questions.promptHtml: Beyond a CPU profile, which JFR events do you use to diagnose latency, and how do you add your own application events?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers use JFR as a correlated timeline (GC, locks, I/O, app), not just a flame graph.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I use jdk.GCPhasePause/jdk.GarbageCollection for pauses, jdk.JavaMonitorEnter and jdk.ThreadPark for lock waits, jdk.SocketRead/SocketWrite and jdk.FileRead for I/O, jdk.ObjectAllocationSample for allocation, jdk.ExecutionSample for CPU stacks, and jdk.SafepointBegin/End (or related safepoint events) for stalls. For application context I define a custom Event subclass (for example one per request or per downstream call) so the timeline shows business operations next to the JVM events. I read them with JMC or jfr print.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Events have thresholds: duration events under the threshold are dropped (e.g. monitor enter default 20 ms in default.jfc), so short but frequent waits are invisible until you lower the threshold in a custom .jfc (costs overhead).
  • Custom events: extend jdk.jfr.Event, annotate with @Name, @Label, fields are recorded; call begin(), commit() (commit is cheap when the event is disabled).
  • Event streaming (JDK 14+): RecordingStream lets you subscribe in-process (onEvent("jdk.GarbageCollection", e -> ...)) to export metrics or detect anomalies without file I/O.
  • JDK 21+ adds virtual thread events (e.g. jdk.VirtualThreadPinned, with a threshold), covered in the virtual threads chunk.
  • JDK 25 adds new CPU-time sampling (JEP 509, experimental, Linux): verify before relying on it.
  • Analysis: jfr summary (event counts), jfr print --events X --stack-depth 20, jfr print --json, or JMC's automated analysis rules.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Name("app.DownstreamCall")
@Label("Downstream call")
class DownstreamCall extends Event {
    @Label("Service") String service;
    @Label("Status") int status;
}

DownstreamCall ev = new DownstreamCall();
ev.begin();
try { ev.status = client.call(); } finally { ev.service = "payments"; ev.commit(); }

try (var rs = new RecordingStream()) {
    rs.enable("jdk.GarbageCollection").withoutThreshold();
    rs.onEvent("jdk.GarbageCollection", e -> metrics.record(e.getDuration("sumOfPauses")));
    rs.startAsync();
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Concluding "no lock contention" because default thresholds hide it.
  • Enabling every event at zero threshold in prod.
  • Putting high-cardinality or PII fields in custom events (dumps are shared).
  • Forgetting events are per-thread; you must correlate with the thread/request id you record.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you overlay GC pauses and slow requests? → both are events on one timeline in JMC; correlate timestamps.
  2. Overhead of a custom event? → near zero when disabled; small when enabled, mostly buffer writes.
  3. JFR vs OpenTelemetry tracing? → JFR is JVM-internal causality (what the JVM did), tracing is cross-service causality; use both.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: flame graph in JMC. Senior: picks the specific events for the symptom, knows thresholds, adds custom events and streams them.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A mystery 300 ms stall every minute was a jdk.GCPhasePause plus a long safepoint triggered by a periodic class-redefinition agent; only the multi-event timeline showed it.

questions.contextHtml:
A metrics-enrichment service (JDK 21, 8 vCPU pod, 150 request threads, 1,500 RPS) shows p50 12 ms but p99 1.8 s after a feature added "tenant-level rate counters". CPU is only 30%. Thread count is stable. GC pauses ~15 ms. A sampled jstack shows many threads like:

"http-exec-87" #187 BLOCKED on java.util.HashMap@6a4f (a tenant counter map)
   at com.acme.RateLimiter.record(RateLimiter.java:52)
   - waiting to lock <0x00000007c1a0d2e0> (a java.util.Collections$SynchronizedMap)
"http-exec-12" RUNNABLE
   at java.net.SocketInputStream.socketRead0
   at com.acme.RateLimiter.record(RateLimiter.java:58)
   - locked <0x00000007c1a0d2e0>

The code: synchronized (counters) { counters.merge(tenant, 1, Integer::sum); audit.log(tenant); }, where audit.log makes a blocking call to a remote audit service.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix. Why is CPU low while latency is terrible?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replace HashMap with ConcurrentHashMap." That ignores the remote call made while holding the lock, which would remain the bottleneck.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is audit.log expected to be synchronous? What is the audit service latency (p50/p99)? Does the lock cover all tenants? Any recent audit service slowness?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the audit call via flag or move it out of the lock; if no flag, roll back the feature.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A single global lock held across a remote call serializes all requests (Little's law: if the audit call takes 20 ms, throughput is capped at 50 ops/s per lock; we run 1,500 RPS, so queueing explodes). (b) GC (ruled out). (c) Thread pool exhaustion as a symptom. (d) CPU throttling (CPU low so no).
  4. How I'd verify each: Three thread dumps (jcmd Thread.print -l) to see one holder and many waiters in the same frame; JFR jdk.JavaMonitorEnter events with a lowered threshold to confirm monitor wait durations and the lock class; async-profiler --lock 10ms and wall mode to see time at RateLimiter.record; measure the audit service latency.
  5. Root cause: The monitor on counters is held during a network call. Holder is RUNNABLE in socketRead0, 100+ others BLOCKED. Throughput is bounded by 1 / audit latency; CPU idles because nothing can run. p50 is fine only when the audit service is quick and the queue short.
  6. Fix: Short-term: take the audit call out of the critical section. Long-term:
private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> counters = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
void record(String tenant) {
    counters.computeIfAbsent(tenant, t -> new LongAdder()).increment();
    auditQueue.offer(tenant); // bounded queue, drained by a worker (drop/aggregate on overflow)
}

Also timeouts and a bulkhead for the audit client. Note that computeIfAbsent should have cheap mapping functions. 7. Prevention: Code review rule: no I/O under a lock; jdk.JavaMonitorEnter alert in JFR dashboards; load test with a slow downstream stub. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not just switching to ConcurrentHashMap (the remote call under synchronized would still serialize); not increasing threads (more waiters); async audit means possible loss on crash, so choose at-least-once buffering if audit must be durable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Virtual threads would fix it? → no; in JDK 21 a blocked synchronized holder pins the carrier, and the serialization remains; the lock design is the issue.
  • Audit must be reliable? → write to a local durable log/outbox and ship asynchronously.
  • Fair vs unfair lock? → unrelated; the hold time is the issue.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a "tiny" synchronized block around a Redis call worked until Redis p99 rose to 50 ms during failover; request threads piled up and the whole tier went red with 25% CPU.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swaps map type, adds threads.
  • Hire: identifies lock held across I/O, reads the dump, moves I/O out.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the throughput cap, verifies with JFR/lock profile, discusses durability trade-off and prevention.

questions.promptHtml: What is coordinated omission and how can it make your latency measurements lie?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Benchmarking latency correctly is a senior skill; this is a classic trap in load testing and in ad hoc "p99" claims.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Coordinated omission is when the load generator waits for a slow response before sending the next request, so the stall suppresses the very samples that would have shown the stall. A closed-loop client records one slow request instead of the hundreds that would have arrived during it, so percentiles look far better than reality. Open-loop generators (fixed arrival rate, like wrk2 or k6 constant-arrival-rate executors) and HdrHistogram's correction fix this.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Example: intended rate 1,000 req/s per connection pool; one 2 s pause. A closed-loop single-connection client records 1 slow sample (2,000 ms) and ~1,000 fast ones afterward. In an open-loop world ~2,000 requests would have been issued during the pause and each would see an average ~1 s delay. The p99 should be roughly in the 1-2 s range, not 5 ms.
  • Real users do not wait for each other; arrival is independent of the service's state, so the open-loop model is right for internet traffic.
  • Tools: wrk2 (constant throughput, corrected latencies), k6 constant-arrival-rate executor, Gatling open injection profiles, HdrHistogram recordValueWithExpectedInterval.
  • Related: percentile averaging is invalid (never average p99s across pods; merge histograms), and in-process timers miss queue time before the handler (measure at the load balancer/client).
  • Warm-up: run until JIT and caches stabilize, then measure; separate cold-start tests.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// k6: open-loop arrival rate
export const options = {
  scenarios: { steady: {
    executor: 'constant-arrival-rate', rate: 1000, timeUnit: '1s',
    duration: '10m', preAllocatedVUs: 200, maxVUs: 2000 } },
};

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reporting p99 from a closed-loop ab/simple loop.
  • Averaging per-pod percentiles.
  • Measuring only server-side latency which excludes queueing in the accept backlog/LB.
  • Running the load generator on the same host as the target.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you size the VU pool in k6 so it doesn't throttle itself? → set maxVUs high; watch "dropped iterations".
  2. How do GC pauses interact? → a 500 ms pause produces a burst of delayed requests; open-loop tests expose it, closed-loop hides it.
  3. What do you compare between runs? → same rate, same data, same warm-up, with histograms not averages.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "run JMeter and read p99". Senior: understands the open vs closed loop, merges histograms, measures end-to-end, controls warm-up and noise.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team certified p99 at 40 ms with a closed-loop test; in production with real arrivals the same service showed 900 ms p99 during each GC and compaction cycle.

questions.contextHtml: A payments service (JDK 17, 5 GB heap in a 7 GB pod, Kubernetes) crashed twice in one week with java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. Each time the pod restarted within 40 s and the team has no evidence: no heap dump (the container has no volume for it and the JVM flags were -Xmx5g only), GC logs were stdout lines rotated away, and metrics scraped every 60 s show heap hitting max only in the last minute. You are asked to lead the post-incident review and make the next OOM diagnosable.
questions.promptHtml: What changes do you make, and what do you say about how we'd find the root cause next time?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more memory and monitor." No evidence capture, no learning, and the same blind spot remains.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the heap growth gradual (leak) or sudden (one huge request)? Is the latency worse before the crash? Request payload size limits? Any pattern in time (batch jobs, a specific tenant)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps with a persistent or sufficiently large emptyDir/PVC (dump up to ~5 GB), -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError so the pod restarts cleanly after the dump, plus a pod terminationGracePeriodSeconds/startup consideration. Add a safety limit on request body size and batch sizes as a guardrail.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A slow leak (growing collection, listener, cache without bounds). (b) A spike from a huge request/response (e.g. 200 MB batch). (c) A cache sized without regard to heap. (d) Humongous allocation fragmentation in G1 causing allocation failure with free space left (visible in GC logs).
  4. How I'd verify each: Persistent GC logs (-Xlog:gc*:file=...:filecount=10,filesize=20m), 10-15 s metrics resolution on jvm.gc.live.data.size and jvm.memory.used, continuous JFR with jdk.OldObjectSample and path-to-gc-roots on dump, analysis in MAT of the next dump, and request-size histograms.
  5. Root cause: Unknown today; what I can say is that process failed to preserve evidence. The review's finding is a diagnosability gap as much as the OOM itself.
  6. Fix: Short-term flags and volumes as above, GC logs on persistent storage or shipped to the log platform, alert on post-GC live set > 70% of max and on its slope. Long-term: bounded caches (e.g. Caffeine maximumSize/weight), payload limits, load test with large payloads, a documented OOM runbook (where dumps land, who analyzes, retention).
  7. Prevention: Include "diagnosability checklist" in the service template: dump-on-OOM, GC logs, JFR continuous, NMT optional, metrics at 15 s; restrict dump access because of PII; automatic dump upload to restricted storage and cleanup.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not blaming an individual; not enabling -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError without checking disk (a 5 GB dump on 2 GB ephemeral storage evicts the pod); not setting Xmx = pod limit; not taking dumps on every OOM storm without limiting count.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• OOM kill (exit 137) rather than Java OOM? → no dump is produced; that is the container memory path (see the NMT and container memory question).
  • Dump takes 40 s and probe kills the pod? → relax liveness probe or use ExitOnOutOfMemoryError after the dump completes; the JVM writes the dump before exiting.
  • Dump contains customer data? → treat as sensitive, encrypt, short retention, access control.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite case: after adding dump-on-OOM, the next failure produced a 4.8 GB file whose dominator tree showed a single per-tenant cache holding 3.9 GB. The week-long guessing ended in 20 minutes of analysis.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases memory; no evidence plan.
  • Hire: dump-on-OOM with storage, persistent GC logs, finer metrics.
  • Strong hire: adds leading indicators, guardrails, runbook, security of dumps, and blameless review structure.
